Fundraiser by tyrone thomas : Unite for Digital Fearlessness
tyrone thomas is organizing this fundraiser.
"Use what's in your hand" - Adam Clayton Powell Jr.
Your phone isn't just for posting stories and playing music. That little computer in your pocket has more power than entire governments had 20 years ago. Like the ancient Abhaya Mudra - the fearless hand gesture that banishes fear and offers protection from the "Evil Eye" - we're transforming these devices into something that helps communities meet the coming challenges with a sense of fearlessness, rooted in Free Collaboration and Privacy.
Abhaya started as disaster recovery - how do communities rebuild communication when the towers are down and the power's out? But we realized something profound: the same tools that help neighborhoods coordinate after a hurricane are exactly what we need when authoritarians try to silence us. Like the protective Abhaya Mudra, this system creates a shield against the "evil eye" of surveillance while becoming a helpful digital companion that guides and empowers our communities.
Drawing inspiration from Buckminster Fuller's vision of global cooperation for humanity's benefit, Abhaya is designed as the foundation for communities to work together toward a more equitable future. The ecosystem operates through five interconnected elements:
• Tor + Mobile based Mesh Networks: Messages that flow around censorship like water
• Mesh Based Distributed Storage: Truth that lives everywhere so it can't be destroyed
• Mesh Based Distributed Computation Service: AI-capable shared processing power for communities to solve their own challenges
• Sensor/Peripheral IO: User Controlled Eyes and ears embedded in the network
• Mesh Federation: Connecting local networks into unstoppable global resistance
"The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy." - MLK Jr.
After Hurricane Katrina, communities learned they couldn't wait for official help. Hong Kong protesters used mesh networks when the government tried to cut them off. Iranian women shared videos of police brutality when the state blocked social media. Puerto Ricans coordinated mutual aid through amateur radio when Maria destroyed the grid.
The pattern is clear: when systems fail - whether from natural disasters or deliberate suppression - communities need tools to build their own infrastructure. Communities united in purpose and vision can be powerful.
When you contribute to Abhaya, you're investing in infrastructure that makes communities fearless. No CEO can sell it. No government can buy it. No algorithm can suppress it. No storm can wash it away.
Every dollar helps us turn individual devices into collective power. Like Powell said - we're not waiting for someone to save us. We're using what's already in our hands to build the infrastructure of fearlessness.
Fund the network that makes communities fearless.
We're assembling an international team of developers and engineers who understand that code is power, and power should belong to the people. If you're a technologist looking to put your skills toward meaningful resistance, this is how you push back against authoritarianism and corporate overreach.
• Onion Router, I2P, Freenet protocols
• DevOps/SecOps fluent in Dark Web technologies
This is open-source work with no revenue model - Abhaya is designed to be free for all communities. For technologists feeling the weight of current events, it's a concrete way to turn skills into direct action and fulfill civic duty through code. Ready to put your shoulder to the wheel of progress? Reach out.
Because true community care means building the infrastructure that makes us all fearless.

content:
资料照片：在德国慕尼黑举行的慕尼黑安全会议期间，美国国务卿马尔科·卢比奥与中国外交部长王毅会晤。(2026年2月13日)
美国国务卿马尔科·卢比奥(Marco Rubio)星期三(11月11日)应中方请求，与中国外长王毅通电话，讨论美国总统唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)下星期赴深圳出席亚太经合组织(APEC)领导人会议，以及中国国家主席习近平下月赴佛罗里达州出席二十国集团(G20)峰会的安排。美国国务院在通话纪要中提及，美中俄领导人可能举行三方会晤；中方发布的通话消息则未提及这一可能性。
美国国务院说，卢比奥与王毅重申了两国领导人此前就建立“基于尊重、公平和互惠的建设性战略稳定关系”达成的共识。国务院的通话纪要还说，双方认为，有实质内容的领导人对话有助于推进和平与无核化等目标，“包括在未来任何可能与俄罗斯举行的三方领导人会晤中”。这一措辞提到了三方会晤的可能性，但未宣布会议已经敲定，也没有公布具体议程。
中国外交部称，这次通话“是积极和建设性的”。据中方通报，王毅表示，中美关系目前的稳定势头来之不易，中方愿与美方加强沟通、妥善处理分歧，并相互支持办好今年的APEC和G20领导人会议。通报没有提及俄罗斯或无核化议题。
根据美国国务院发布的一份新闻稿，卢比奥与王毅都认为，领导人对话对于“推动和平与无核化”等目标至关重要。另一个特别引人注目的要点是新闻稿提及特朗普、习近平和俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京(Vladimir Putin)有可能在深圳举行三方会晤，而且“和平与无核化”也会包含在三边峰会讨论的议题之内。
APEC领导人会议定于11月18日至19日在深圳举行。特朗普总统此前表示，预计将在会议期间与习近平和俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京(Vladimir Putin)会面，并希望讨论无核化等问题。不过，三国领导人是否举行三方会晤，仍有待正式确认。
核议题可能是筹备三方会晤时的一项分歧。美俄《新削减战略武器条约》(New START)在今年2月4日到期后，双方已不再受该条约规定的战略核武器数量上限约束。卢比奥国务卿曾表示，美国目前倾向于推动包含中国在内的全新多边核军备控制框架。特朗普总统曾表示，他希望与习近平及普京讨论去核化问题；不过，中方尚未确认核军控议题是否会纳入可能的三方会晤议程。
北京则一直认为，中国的核力量与美俄不在同一量级，现阶段要求中国参加三边核裁军谈判“不公平、不合理、不可行”。美国国务院此次使用的“无核化”(denuclearization)一词，并未具体说明拟讨论的是核裁军协议，还是范围更广的核问题。
乌克兰此前已对可能举行的美中俄三方会晤表达关切。乌克兰外长安德里·西比哈(Andrii Sybiha)10月表示，乌美俄领导人会谈可能有助于结束战争，而美中俄领导人会谈可能产生相反效果。乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基(Volodymyr Zelenskyy)也在此前的采访中说，如果会晤讨论乌克兰问题，乌方希望事先得到征询。
“如果乌克兰议题被列入议程，我们希望各方能就此征求乌克兰的意见。至于其他方面，我无法置评，因为我不知道他们具体会讨论什么，”泽连斯基说。

title: The CEO, the Spy, and a Crisis for AI
zh_title: 首席执行官、间谍和人工智能的危机
summary: 在此订阅：Apple 播客 | Spotify | YouTube |阴天 | Pocket Casts 于美国东部时间 2026 年 11 月 12 日上午 9:05 更新 有关第二起妥协事件的报道可能会导致 Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 的毁灭，尽管第一起事件是与一名所谓的中国间谍发生的。本周早些时候，科技巨头们竭尽全力将英伟达的丑闻最小化。埃隆·马斯克表示，黄承认与一名所谓的外国特工有染，但他是“不可替代的”。总统说，黄有可能将商业秘密和国家安全置于危险之中，但他是一个“值得尊敬的人”。
content:
在此订阅：Apple 播客 | Spotify | YouTube |阴天 | Pocket Casts 于美国东部时间 2026 年 11 月 12 日上午 9:05 更新 有关第二起妥协事件的报道可能会导致 Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 的毁灭，尽管第一起事件是与一名所谓的中国间谍发生的。本周早些时候，科技巨头们竭尽全力将英伟达的丑闻最小化。埃隆·马斯克表示，黄承认与一名所谓的外国特工有染，但他是“不可替代的”。特朗普总统表示，黄有可能将商业秘密和国家安全置于危险之中，但他是一个“值得尊敬的人”，而且“他可能有一个借口”。亿万富翁对冲基金经理比尔·阿克曼 (Bill Ackman) 在 X 上发布“前进”，暗示：继续前进——这里没什么可看的。黄似乎太大而不能倒。感兴趣的各方更愿意忽视这些明显的危险，而不是思考失去这个对人工智能繁荣中心的公司如此独特的人可能意味着什么，该公司是如此重要，以至于它目前可能正在支撑美国经济。直到昨天，黄仁勋与一位直接向他汇报的英伟达高管发生了第二次恋情的消息传出后，情况一直如此。英伟达董事会开会考虑黄仁勋的未来，《大西洋月刊》特约撰稿人查理·沃泽尔将此举描述为“从人工智能塔中取出叠叠乐”。目前，黄某已辞职。
负责报道情报机构的特约撰稿人肖恩·哈里斯 (Shane Harris) 和负责报道科技行业的沃泽尔 (Warzel) 在大西洋广播电台上讨论了间谍活动和商业活动。哈里斯考虑了中国可能如何实现这一目标，以及他们可能获得了哪些秘密。沃泽尔认为，如果没有其领导者，英伟达的未来以及更广泛的人工智能繁荣可能会是什么样子。大西洋广播电台的这一集是在英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋辞职前录制的。以下是该集的文字记录： 汉娜·罗辛 (Hanna Rosin)：本周的科技新闻始于詹姆斯·邦德 (James Bond)，但现在更像是 HBO 的《继承之战》(Succession) 的一季。周末有消息称，全球最重要科技公司最重要的核心人物黄仁勋承认与一名疑似中国间谍的女性有染。硅谷泰坦们为黄仁勋辩护，他的公司英伟达是人工智能热潮的引擎。特朗普总统称他为“值得尊敬的人”，但基本上对此不屑一顾。埃隆·马斯克称他为“不可替代的”。亿万富翁对冲基金经理比尔·阿克曼 (Bill Ackman) 在 X 上写道：“前进”，意思是：这里没什么可看的——继续前进。本周早些时候，讨论的主题是所有这些重要人物是否都在为黄进行辩护，因为他对美国经济太重要、太核心，以至于不能考虑失败。太大而不能失败。但突然之间，他就不再是了。我是汉娜·罗辛；这是大西洋广播电台。周三，又传出另一起婚外情的消息。
这一次不是与间谍合作，而是与向黄报告的英伟达高管合作。伟大的人可能很混乱，但显然不会混乱到冒着股价下跌、甚至可能拖垮整个市场的风险。据报道，英伟达董事会开会考虑他的未来，据《华尔街日报》报道，他们正准备罢免他。为了理解这个故事——国际间谍活动、科技经济的影响，所有这一切——我打电话给《大西洋月刊》的两位特约撰稿人：谢恩·哈里斯（Shane Harris），他多年来一直撰写有关间谍和情报世界的文章；查理·沃泽尔（Charlie Warzel），他报道科技并主持《亚特兰蒂斯》

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Updated at 9:05 a.m. ET on November 12, 2026 Reports of a second compromising affair may be the undoing of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, even though the first affair was with an alleged Chinese spy. Earlier this week, tech titans were going out of their way to minimize the scandal at Nvidia. Huang had confessed to an affair with an alleged foreign agent, but he was “irreplaceable,” according to Elon Musk. Huang had potentially put trade secrets and national security at risk, but he was an “honorable guy,” said President Trump, and “he probably has an excuse for it.” The billionaire hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman posted on X, “Onward,” implying: Move along—nothing to see here . Huang, it seemed, was too big to fail. Interested parties were more willing to ignore the obvious dangers than contemplate what it might mean to lose the man so singularly identified with the company at the center of the AI boom, the company so important that it might be currently propping up the U.S. economy. That was true until yesterday, when news broke of a second affair Huang had, with an executive at Nvidia who reports directly to him. Nvidia’s board met to consider Huang’s future, a move that the Atlantic staff writer Charlie Warzel describes as “taking a Jenga block out” of the AI tower. Now Huang has resigned. The staff writers Shane Harris, who covers intelligence agencies, and Warzel, who covers the tech industry, discuss on Radio Atlantic both the espionage and the business. Harris considers how China might have pulled this off, and what secrets they might have obtained. Warzel considers what the future of Nvidia, and the AI boom more broadly, might look like without its leader. This episode of Radio Atlantic taped before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: The tech news this week started out James Bond , but is now shaping up to be more like a season of HBO’s Succession . Over the weekend, news broke that Jensen Huang, the most important man at the center of the most important tech company in the world, admitted to having an affair with a woman who is a suspected Chinese spy. Titans of Silicon Valley defended Huang, whose company, Nvidia, is the engine of the AI boom. President Trump called him an ”honorable guy,” essentially shrugging it off. Elon Musk called him “irreplaceable.” Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman wrote on X, “Onward,” as in: Nothing to see here—move along. Earlier this week, the discussion was about whether all these VIPs were defending Huang because he was just too important, too central to the American economy, to contemplate losing. Too big to fail. And then all of a sudden, he wasn’t. I’m Hanna Rosin; this is Radio Atlantic . On Wednesday, news of another affair broke. This one was not with a spy but with an Nvidia executive who reports to Huang. Great men can be messy, but apparently not so messy that they risk tanking their stock and potentially taking down the entire market with them. The Nvidia board reportedly met to consider his future and, according to The Wall Street Journal , they are preparing to oust him. To make sense of this story—the international espionage, the fallout for the tech economy, all of it—I called up two Atlantic staff writers: Shane Harris, who has written for years about spies and the intelligence world, and Charlie Warzel, who covers tech and hosts the Atlantic podcast Galaxy Brain. Shane, welcome back to the show. Shane Harris: Thank you, Hanna. Rosin: Charlie, welcome back. Charlie Warzel: Thank you very much. Rosin: All right, Charlie, we’re gonna start with you. Jensen Huang is not exactly a household name yet. He and his leather jackets are not quite at the level of Steve Jobs and his black turtlenecks. And yet by some accounts, including yours, he seems to hold the fate of the universe, or at least this country, in his hands. Can you explain why that is and who he is? Warzel: So Jensen Huang is the CEO and he’s also the co-founder of Nvidia. Nvidia makes processing units, GPUs, which is essentially the thing that allows the AI boom to happen. It helps power the data centers; it helps train the models. Without them, you don’t have generative AI, but you also don’t have things like computer graphics and graphics cards. Huang is very good at seeing around corners, and is idolized for seeing the AI boom happening and reorienting the company around the idea of making better and better and more efficient chips and getting them to the right people. So he is the head of arguably the most important company in artificial intelligence, and that is because the U.S. economy hinges on the AI boom right now. The Magnificent Seven, which is the seven massive technology companies, they are responsible for roughly a third of the S&P 500’s value at the moment. And Nvidia is the crucial node of all of that. So, according to The Economist , Nvidia’s stock produced 15 cents for every dollar that the American stock market has returned since ChatGPT came out. They are one of the most valuable companies in the entire world because of this. And what they do—and this is why he’s so important—what Nvidia does is: It takes a lot of that money, and then it has become arguably the primary investor in the rest of the artificial-intelligence industry. As of July, they have had $99 billion worth of investments, and they invest in OpenAI; they invest in SpaceX, Anthropic; they invest in data-center providers. They put all this money into an ecosystem so that those people can then purchase more Nvidia chips. And it’s part of what people who are concerned that there might be an artificial-intelligence bubble say is a “circular mode of financing.” And so the feeling about why Jensen is so important is he is the person who steered the company that, if it imploded, it would bring the entire economy down with it. Rosin: So that brings us to the most recent news. Jensen Huang is critical to Nvidia. Nvidia is critical to the U.S. economy, and now the board is reportedly preparing to oust him. So what does that mean? Warzel: It’s honestly unprecedented. I really don't know what to think about this, because this was never in the cards. Jensen Huang is Nvidia; Nvidia is Jensen Huang. You really can’t separate the two, and now the whole world and the stock market is being asked to separate the two. We’re in uncharted territory right now. Rosin: Is there any precedent? Is there anything that we can look to, to try and understand this moment? Warzel: Well, an interesting thing here, as we are talking in the middle of this chaos, is the fact that some of this happened a couple years ago with Sam Altman and OpenAI. Sam Altman was ousted by the board. They brought in the CEO of Twitch, the streaming company, or the former CEO. It was this big debacle, and everyone was just absolutely flabbergasted that, Oh my gosh, Sam Altman has been ousted here. What’s gonna happen? And then you cut to a couple days later; he reversed it. He came back. This whole cycle was almost for naught, but then Sam had consolidated power at the end. And that is a hard thing for all of us to get out of our heads in this moment from tech observers. Rosin : Right, because maybe this story’s not over yet. Warzel: It seems plausible that it’s not over, and that’s because there’s so much baggage with Jensen in terms of all the deals that he’s involved in. He is the person who has brokered all of these investments across the AI industry, and the people who know him say he does this on a handshake. He is the central character of all of Nvidia’s success. Rosin: Okay, so Jensen Huang is the central character in this story. Another character, of course, is Alice Huang, who is no relation. That’s the woman he had an affair with, who is described by U.S. officials as a “Chinese intelligence asset.” Shane, what does that mean exactly? How is that the same or different from being a spy? Harris: It’s practically not all that different, right? So in this case, what it suggests is that she is somebody who is providing information to China’s Ministry of State Security. So that’s what an asset is. Whether or not she is actually an officer in Chinese state security—as in, employed by them directly—is unknown. The allegation here is that her job was to provide information to Chinese intelligence officials about what she was learning from Jensen Huang in the course of their relationship together, which was described as being intimate. It’s not clear whether or not Alice Huang—who, by the way, is not related to Jensen Huang, we should say—was recruited as somebody to go out and target Jensen Huang and try to get close to him, or whether the Chinese intelligence agency knew that she was already close to Jensen Huang and went to her and then persuaded her to share information with them. It is typical for the MSS, the Ministry of State Security—it’s China’s equivalent of the CIA—to find people like that, who have access to people who they wanna know about, and to coerce them into working for MSS. It’s not about going out and saying, Could you do a solid for the government of China? It’s more like, If you don’t cooperate, ugly things might happen to you . Rosin: So on the one hand, you’re describing something that China does routinely. When you read about this, were you thinking, Oh, this is just a Tuesday in Chinese spying, or is this a big deal in some way? Harris: Well, I would say that the tactics are pretty common, and China is extraordinarily aggressive and pervasive in their attempts to steal and obtain technology and intellectual property from U.S. companies. They’ve been doing that for decades. They do a lot of it through hacking. Where this operation is extraordinary is in who the target is—arguably one of the most important CEOs in the world, who, as Charlie has said, is absolutely central to the biggest industry right now, the race that China is trying to win against the United States. And not only that, he’s a personal friend of the president of the United States. He talks to him. He influences his thinking on AI. For any intelligence agency to place an asset in that situation with access to those kinds of people, that’s a home run in the spy game. Rosin: So a big win for China, a huge revelation. Charlie, how does the tech world initially respond to this news? Warzel: The entire conversation around artificial intelligence, and the fears that a lot of people who are building this technology have with what they are building, the concerns that it’s going to lead to job loss or AI-agent swarms that are going to be able to hack or develop bioweapons—all of these risks are justified by this industry because of the fact that we are in a geopolitical race against China. Rosin: Yes! Yes. Warzel: China should not develop this technology before us. And even if we incur some terrible, almost existential-level risks , the thinking goes, the logic goes, it’s better for us to be in charge of those than China to be in charge of those . And so now what you have is the man at the center of the AI boom, who, it turns out, has had a romantic relationship with a Chinese asset. And the initial impulse, especially this weekend in Silicon Valley amongst a lot of people—including Elon Musk, but some other venture capitalists—was to either joke about and make light of, or to suggest that this is not that big of a deal, or that really, this is being seen as some awful moral infraction. But really, people: It’s not right, but people do cheat on their spouses . And in their justification, it was that Jensen is a great innovator and a good person who would not do anything to compromise national security, and therefore, I trust that this is all going to work out . Which is a very odd thing if your No. 1 concern in the industry is beating China. You’d think you’d be a lot more concerned about this than a lot of people in Silicon Valley have been. Rosin: Yeah, you would think. I remember in the article you wrote earlier this week, you quoted billionaire hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman, who wrote on X, “Onward,” as in: Move along everyone—there’s nothing to see here. And then, of course, there’s Donald Trump, who just called Huang an “honorable guy,” as if to minimize the whole thing. So obviously with news that the Nvidia board reportedly tried to oust him, people did not just easily move along. But I wonder if you can explain why people at first tried so hard to push this “onward” mentality. Because it was strange. Warzel: I think the reason for this “onward” mentality, this let’s not look too hard at this at the moment mentality, is about Huang’s centrality to the global economy right now. I think that there is a huge fear. I you just look politically at Donald Trump, first and foremost, you can make a very good case that the economy has not absolutely cratered in his second term because of the investment in artificial intelligence, that the entire stock market, one of the things that Donald Trump cares about the most, is hinging on this. And the idea of Jensen Huang having to step down because he has become this huge risk to the company reputationally, or that he has divulged something that is going to hurt the United States’ position, both in innovation and national-security-wise—all of that could lead to Nvidia’s stock plummeting, for them not to be able to invest as much money into this, for there to be a larger technology-stock sell-off. And the position is so precarious that it is in Donald Trump’s best interest to not get out over his skis and call for his resignation or call for investigations to learn even more and more about this. And if you’re all of these folks in Silicon Valley whose portfolios are wrapped up in this, who are making a civilizationally historical bet financially on an industry, it’s also not in your best interest to have Jensen Huang, a person who doesn’t really have a clear successor, a person who is so fundamentally in control of that company—it doesn’t really make sense for them to have him step down or be pressured into this, or for more to come out about this that makes this look even worse. Rosin: Alright, so that was the initial reaction at the beginning of the week. But, of course, more has come out. On Wednesday, there were reports of another affair—not with a spy, this one with an Nvidia executive that reports to Huang. And then later that day, the board reportedly met to consider his future and, according to The Wall Street Journal , they are preparing to oust him. What do you make about how things developed? How something that people were trying to push away and deny for days and days and days, then suddenly actually happens. Warzel: Well, I think what you can see from the reaction online from a lot of tech executives and tech people, there’s a lot of wanting the board to hold strong here. Rosin: And what is “hold strong”? Do you mean hold strong in the way that confidence is important in the market? Like showing confidence, showing that there’s not chaos? Warzel: There’s an idea, essentially, that shareholders here do not want Jensen removed. Shareholders don’t care about the morality of this thing. Maybe they don’t even care about the national-security implications of the whole spy part of this. But the idea that the second affair has shown up—the feeling from a lot of these investor types and Silicon Valley types is that what matters most is that we win the AI race. What matters most is that Jensen is there. What matters most is that this person who has the favor of so many people in Silicon Valley and these relationships and is the deal maker when it comes to chips stays in place. Not only because of the market, but just because there’s so much uncertainty there. And so there’s a lot of hope that—I saw online that—the board would hold strong. But I’ve seen Elon Musk joking about offering a job to Jensen. I’ve seen a lot of people basically saying, We have to pick this person up . We have to figure out something to do. Or that this would be some kind of coordinated attack either in the media, or from China, or somebody else. The second revelation coming out has to be nefarious in some way in order to undermine the American position in A.I. So I don’t think, from that perspective, you’re seeing anything other than, again, still more circling of the wagons. Rosin: Wait, so you’re saying they’re still supporting him? Even if the board tries to oust him, even if it becomes impossible not to oust him, the Silicon Valley mentality will still be, He’s the great man. We have to keep him alive . Warzel: I think that there is a feeling that the ouster of Jensen Huang is a massive mistake. It’s people succumbing to a lot of pressure here, or a coordinated campaign in some way. I think that is really how a lot of people feel, or that there’s gonna have to be some place where he comes in and he settles, after the dust settles back in this ecosystem, because he’s such a crucial, important part of it. But I think where it’s all coming from, very truly, is a place of fear, is a place of uncertainty, of what could happen if he is removed from this ecosystem where he is such a crucial node. Rosin: It’s kind of incredible how Silicon Valley exalts and protects its geniuses, even when they behave like fools. It is incredible. Warzel : Well, I think the thing here that I’m seeing from certain people—again, on X.com, but these are real people—who are saying things like, Morality is one thing, but this thing that we're building is another. This is an opportunity . This is a crucial moment. This is a national-security imperative —which is funny because of everything that happened with the Chinese spy. That, We mere mortals, our judgment doesn't matter here because it’s bigger than that. And I think we see this again, and again, and again in the industry—that these people are doing things that are so big that they are beyond reproach. Rosin: Wow. I really like that answer, Charlie. I find that surprising, but not surprising. Warzel: There are people, clearly—the board is making a decision, which stands for something. The pressure is clearly there. And I think what the Silicon Valley part of this discussion always misses, or is missing in this moment, at the very least, is the fact he has not disclosed another affair. Now it’s come out, and this is an affair with a major client and a direct report. And those things, just as a CEO and as somebody running an organization, are a very big deal outside of the whole A.I. supply chain and national security of it all . Rosin: Okay, Shane, that’s the view in Silicon Valley. No matter how Jensen Huang’s story unfolds, the intelligence community will still want to know more. What are the big questions they continue to have? Harris: The question is, what information did Alice Huang actually provide to the MSS? Did she find some compelling information about trade secrets, technology development, market strategy? Or was what she was providing really not all that interesting, and really not all that revealing? Now, the president, according to news reports, was informed that Jensen Huang was close to Alice Huang, and that she was suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. In my experience, officials in the intelligence community would not brief the president on that kind of minutiae—granted, this is a VVIP we’re talking about here—unless they were pretty concerned about that relationship. Now, we shouldn’t infer too much from that, but I would imagine that if they thought that this relationship was harmless and Alice Huang was passing back nothing of interest to the MSS, that they wouldn’t alert the president about it. The second thing is that, as far as we know, no one in the U.S. government ever briefed him on the fact that his girlfriend was a Chinese asset. Now, usually when the FBI or another agency chooses not to give someone what’s called a “defensive briefing” (i.e., You should know that your girlfriend is not who she says she is; be careful ), it’s because they’re worried about that disclosure cutting off their access to the intelligence that they’re getting. So in this case, it looks like they developed intelligence that Alice Huang was spying for the MSS. They could have learned that by monitoring people she was talking to in the MSS, and they’re worried that if they tell Jensen Huang about her intelligence relationship, that blows up the entire channel of information. It tips off the Chinese that they’re being spied on. All of this I mention to point out that I think that the intelligence community’s view on this was probably, This is serious , right? This is significant. [ Music ] Rosin: After the break, exactly what information could Alice Huang have gotten from him? And what’s the future of Nvidia? [ Break ] Rosin: This story of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang has a lot of unanswered questions: What is up with her former company, Megaspeed? How did she rise to power? How did they even meet? But for Charlie, something he kept wondering about was the timing of it all. Warzel: One thing that I will say about this story that, to me, is really wild, and I think opens up a bunch of questions, is that The New York Times , back last October 2025, essentially reported out this entire story. The romantic-relationship part of it was not disclosed. And Huang had not released a statement saying that he had been unfaithful to his wife and he’s sorry. But this story was out there, and I’m covering this industry. It didn’t really percolate to the top of my radar. This did not break through in this way, and I think that that is very fascinating. Right now we are in a really interesting position because we don’t yet know what we need to know about this company, Megaspeed, about Alice Huang’s actual influence. Frankly, the real issue here is in regards to: What did this relationship do in terms of what China had access to? And I think that we’re only in the first or second inning on all of that. Harris: Another reason that’s so important is that Megaspeed is set up to take advantage essentially of a loophole in U.S. chip policy towards China, which is, Okay, we’re not gonna sell the most advanced chips to China, but we will sell them to a company that sets up in another country and operates a data center that then rents that capacity to China . So she’s already kind of navigating in this vulnerable space that U.S. policy towards China doesn’t account for. And the fact that she then, or is already, a Chinese intelligence asset just adds to probably the concern that I could imagine U.S. officials would have had, because her company essentially exists to make money by circumventing the very policies the U.S. is trying to create to keep China from getting ahead in the AI race. Rosin: What would China have demanded of Alice Huang? What would have been the list they gave to Alice Huang, like, We want X , Y , and Z? Harris: You could imagine it would be pretty long, but maybe some that would be at the top: What’s the next-generation chip that’s coming, and how powerful is it? What are the conversations going on inside the Trump administration about where they might be amenable to loosening the restrictions on the sales of chips to us? Can you implant this idea in Jensen Huang’s head that he should go to the president and say X , Y , or Z ? It’s tempting to say, Tell us everything that you can , right? But if she’s an asset who’s being directed, there will be pretty specific things that China wants to know, and that list will be curated by all of the different people in that space in China who have an objective, which might be getting access to better chips or trying to understand what the next wave of technological development is so that they can get ahead of that. Warzel: Well, I also think, too—we don’t know the exact relationship between Alice and Jensen: how often they met, and in which places they met, whether they were alone or not. Was she alone with his phone? There are things like that. He is call buddies with Donald Trump. What potentially does she have access to? Are the Nvidia IT and device policies as strict when he is in Singapore as they are when he is in the United States? There’s so many questions about that. There’s potential for things like data collection in there. He has god-tier access to his own company, presumably. I think everything is on the table, is essentially the point. Rosin: Charlie, I’m curious what the fear of China getting ahead looks like from inside the tech industry. I understand why the U.S. government fears it. How do tech leaders talk about that? Warzel: Well, I think one of the fears of China getting ahead is that China is also much more inclined to have these open-source models—these models that you don’t have to pay for in the same way that level the playing field, so to speak, between the OpenAIs and the Anthropics of the world, in which they are charging a pretty penny, especially for enterprise access. When the Chinese model DeepSeek came onto the scene sort of unannounced, and showed that it was just as powerful, if not in some cases a little more powerful, than some of the, quote, unquote, “frontier models” from these American companies, it called briefly into question the entire economic model of all of these companies. But I think the way that these AI companies—they call themselves “labs”—the way that they work is: They train, they build up these models, then they release them to the public. But the things that they are training tend to be a lot more powerful. And those models can be very dangerous if they’re released to different people, but also if they’re used in any kind of way. And so the idea is: If China were to leapfrog the U.S. in the capability with the training and the things like this, they would be playing effectively a different game. And the capabilities can work in an exponential fashion. And so if you are six months ahead, that doesn’t sound like a lot to most people on the outside of this business, but it could mean living in a completely different paradigm of the technology. Rosin: Shane, is there a worst-case scenario, like: We find out X happens, and everything falls apart ? In this moment when all this information is emerging, what would be the “Oh my God” scenario? Harris: One would be: The president was told Jensen Huang has relayed private discussions that the two of you had to this woman, and she has delivered it gift-wrapped to Chinese intelligence, and they know what our AI policy is gonna be next year . And the president said , Eh, whatever . And that he did nothing about it. The president’s lack of response to what he was told, reportedly, twice, begs the question of, Well, what exactly was he told? So that’s one. Another worst-case scenario could be when Alice Huang is in a private room hanging out with Jensen Huang and he gets up to excuse himself for a few minutes and she puts a device on his computer, and the MSS is up entirely in the communications of the CEO of Nvidia for the past year and a half and sees everything that’s going across his email. The intelligence agency would be crazy not to at least contemplate trying to do that if they had an asset with intimate contact to someone like Jensen Huang. So those would be worst-case scenarios. That essentially, China, either through direct access to his devices or because he is, in the course of pillow talk, talking about trade secrets or his conversations with White House officials, that that’s all going back to Beijing, and they’re basically just sitting there and reading it. [ Music ] Rosin: Charlie, and listeners, I’m going to do something a little unusual now. We actually taped another version of this conversation earlier on Tuesday, before the latest news broke. And I want to play you a bit of the audio from that taping. So this is Charlie, on Charlie. Charlie, are we ready for Charlie? Warzel: ( Laughs .) Always. Always ready for myself. Rosin: ( Laughs .) Okay, go ahead. Warzel: Well, it’s funny because when you were asking Shane that question of what’s the worst scenario, my version of it is that there’s no choice but for Huang to step down. I think that’s a nightmare scenario for the economy, also probably for Nvidia. I think it’s very important to think about Huang in the sense of this entire boom. And going back to what I said at the outset of this is that he is believed to be one of the visionaries who’s made this happen, whose decisions in changing Nvidia’s supply chain, but also in utilizing how these chips can power this artificial-intelligence investment and scale things up—he is credited with a lot of that. He is extremely well respected. And the confidence collapse that happens when you take that person out of it, I think it would at least cause some very, very serious turmoil. And I think one way to look at all of this—especially if you’re a cynic about the AI build-out—is that it is, if not a house of cards, it is a Jenga pile, right? Or it is something in which there are so many load-bearing bricks, and if you take one of them out, the whole thing can come tumbling down. And I think it’s not a ridiculous thing to say that Nvidia is one of those load-bearing bricks. [ Music ] Rosin: Charlie, that nightmare scenario you describe might suddenly be happening now. So what do you think? Warzel: I think that no one should have to listen to themselves from two days ago, frankly. Rosin: ( Laughs .) Warzel: I think that this is a little bit of a scary moment. Maybe it’s scarier than we think. I wanna separate the morality of what he’s done here, and the recklessness of what he’s done, from just the meat and potatoes—like how the market and how this industry might react. I’ve heard of Nvidia being referred to as the “bank of Nvidia,” recently, since this has come out—this idea that they put so much investment into this sector, and that so much of that investment in this sector is so closely tied to his ability, Jensen’s ability, to make these deals. But the fact that this industry is funded and supplied by this one guy in this one company, and the idea of him not being at the center of it is fully destabilizing, I think. I really and truly believe that. This analyst, Dan Ives, said that Nvidia would be worth 25 percent to 30 percent less without Jensen Huang. This may be the craziest story in the AI era since ChatGPT launched, truly. What I sense and what I hear from people in the industry about all of this is that we have taken one of the Jenga blocks out, potentially, and does the tower hold up? Does it not? We’re gonna find out in the next weeks and months. Rosin: Well, Charlie, Shane, thank you so much for joining me today. Harris: Thank you. Warzel: Thanks for having me. Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Rosie Hughes and Jinae West. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

title: Rethinking the pipeline for critical defense electronics

summary: 军事需要近乎实时地应对新出现的威胁，这给新能力交付作战人员之前建立在漫长的研究、开发、测试和评估 (RDT&E) 周期之上的传统采购流程带来了压力。这一点在射频 (RF) 技术中最为明显，快速变化的电子战 (EW) 威胁、指挥和控制的新通信要求以及不断扩大的任务正在迫使国防工业基地在更短的时间内提供更多的能力。挑战不仅仅在于设计更快的处理器或更高的速度
content:
军事需要近乎实时地应对新出现的威胁，这给新能力交付作战人员之前建立在漫长的研究、开发、测试和评估 (RDT&E) 周期之上的传统采购流程带来了压力。这一点在射频 (RF) 技术中最为明显，快速变化的电子战 (EW) 威胁、指挥和控制的新通信要求以及不断扩大的任务正在迫使国防工业基地在更短的时间内提供更多的能力。

挑战不仅仅在于设计更快的处理器或更强大的射频放大器。例如，国防电子设备必须满足自主平台日益严格的尺寸、重量、功率和热限制，同时保持适应新的波形、频率和操作要求。与此同时，供应链限制和生产计划是这些系统到达作战人员手中的速度的决定因素。

对于向主要承包商供应电子产品的公司来说，答案越来越多地涉及采用经过验证的设计，而不是从头开始开发每项功能。这种方法降低了技术风险，缩短了资格认证时间，并且更容易将新功能集成到现有平台中。
Frontgrade Technologies [Frontgrade] 高级副总裁兼首席技术官 Lorne Graves 表示：“我们没有时间部署整个平台，回来看看会发生什么，然后再去做另一个。” “那些日子已经一去不复返了。”

**比传统获取更快地适应威胁**

如前所述，技术变革的步伐与开发、鉴定和生产军用电子产品所需的时间之间不匹配。对于电子战、战术通信、雷达和太空应用中使用的射频系统，在传统采集周期中，要求可能会发生很大变化。为一种威胁环境开发的架构在部署时可能需要适应不同的频率、波形或操作条件。

这就非常重视适应性强的硬件和设计，这些硬件和设计允许在不更换整个子系统的情况下引入新功能。

“响应这些威胁所需的时间意味着你不会部署该平台，”格雷夫斯说。 “该架构最好具有适应性，能够改变和应对这些威胁。”
这种适应性并​​不是来自于针对每项需求追求高度定制的解决方案。相反，该解决方案越来越多地应用商业开发的功能和现有的合格设计，“以有效地获得足够好的解决方案，而无需创建非常定制的解决方案来满足非常有限的一组要求，”Frontgrade 高级副总裁兼首席增长官 Jack Kilian 说。

实际上，这可能意味着从已经满足 80% 的程序要求的设计开始，然后调整特定的功能、接口或性能特征。 Kilian 表示，它还可能涉及通过“相似性”进行鉴定，利用现有设计的证据来减少相关配置所需的测试。

对于军方来说，其优势不仅仅是缩短采购时间，因为它有助于更​​快地将演进的能力引入战场，同时为威胁变化时的后续升级保留路径。

采用经过验证的设计来满足需求，加快您的速度

【原文 English Original】
Military necessity to respond to emerging threats in near-real time is putting pressure on a traditional acquisition process built on lengthy Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation (RDT&E) cycles before a new capability can pass to warfighters. Nowhere is that more apparent than in radio frequency (RF) technology, where rapidly changing electronic warfare (EW) threats, new communications requirements for command and control, and expanding missions are forcing the defense industrial base to deliver more capability in less time.

The challenge extends beyond designing faster processors or more powerful RF amplifiers. Defense electronics must meet increasingly demanding size, weight, power, and thermal constraints for autonomous platforms, for example, while remaining adaptable to new waveforms, frequencies, and operational requirements. At the same time, supply-chain limitations and production schedules are the determining factor in how quickly those systems reach the warfighter.

For companies supplying electronics to prime contractors, the answer increasingly involves adapting proven designs rather than developing every capability from scratch. That approach reduces technical risk, shortens qualification timelines, and makes it easier to integrate new functionality into existing platforms.

“We don’t have time to field an entire platform, come back, see what happens, go do another one,” said Lorne Graves, senior vice president and chief technology officer at Frontgrade Technologies [Frontgrade]. “Those days are gone.”

**Adapting to threats faster than traditional acquisition allows**

As mentioned, there’s a mismatch between the pace of technological change and the time required to develop, qualify, and produce military electronics. For RF systems used in EW, tactical communications, radar, and space applications, requirements can change considerably during a traditional acquisition cycle. An architecture developed for one threat environment may need to accommodate different frequencies, waveforms, or operating conditions by the time it is fielded.

That puts a premium on adaptable hardware and designs that allow new capabilities to be introduced without replacing an entire subsystem.

“The time it takes to respond to these threats means that you wouldn’t field the platform,” said Graves. “The architecture better have adaptability to be able to change and counter those threats.”

Such adaptability doesn’t come from pursuing highly customized solutions for every requirement. Rather, the solution is increasingly the application of commercially developed capabilities and existing qualified designs “to effectively get a good enough solution without having to create a very bespoke solution to meet a very narrow set of requirements,” said Jack Kilian, senior vice president and chief growth officer for Frontgrade.

In practice, that could mean beginning with a design that already meets 80 percent of a program’s requirements, then adapting particular functions, interfaces, or performance characteristics. It could also involve qualification by “similarity”, using evidence from an existing design to reduce the testing needed for a related configuration, according to Kilian.

For the military, the advantage is not simply a shorter procurement timeline as it facilitates the bringing of evolved capabilities to the field sooner while preserving a path for subsequent upgrades as the threat changes.

Adapting proven designs to meet needs speeds up the delivery timeline for new technologies. (Photo illustration courtesy of Frontgrade.)

**Supply chain resilience becomes part of the mission**

The same emphasis on speed is changing how electronics suppliers manage manufacturing capacity. RF systems depend on specialized semiconductors, materials, and mechanical components that can be difficult to source. Gallium nitride, widely used in high-performance RF applications, illustrates the challenge because of supply-chain exposure involving the raw gallium required for its production.

Kilian noted the concentration of gallium production in China and the export restrictions that have increased concerns about access to critical materials. Bearings, magnets, and other components can also create lengthy production delays.

Frontgrade is addressing those risks through multiple sourcing, strategic inventories of critical parts, and greater internal manufacturing capability. The company is qualifying additional suppliers to reduce dependence on individual manufacturers, and maintaining stocks of components used across multiple product lines so production teams can respond more quickly without committing inventory to a single, specialized design. Standardizing certain components across products can substantially shorten delivery schedules.

“It can significantly pull in these lead times from beyond 52 weeks to below 26 weeks in many cases for these deliverables,” said Kilian. That means, for example, that Frontgrade can get critical hardware and electronics into a prime contractor’s hands for integration onto a communications satellite.

**Integrating the electronics backbone**

Frontgrade’s advanced RF capabilities have expanded through the addition of Aethercomm (acquired in 2023), IDSI (the Defense Solutions division of Crescend Technologies acquired in 2025), and Tricom Research (2025), complementing its existing portfolio of antennas, radiation-hardened electronics, processing, and power technologies.

Together, those capabilities cover a substantial portion of the signal chain from RF signal acquisition and conditioning through conversion, digital processing, and storage – whether they be individual components or larger integrated systems.

“Our prime customers are looking for partners that can effectively deliver integrated subsystem solutions that are ready to layer their application software on top of it,” said Kilian, noting in that arrangement that suppliers like Frontgrade can deliver hardware together with the middleware and application programming interfaces needed to support higher-level software integration.

Customers can purchase components to build their own boards, obtain board-level subsystems, or use more complete integrated systems that already combine RF, digital conversion, processing, and storage. The objective is to let prime contractors concentrate on the application and mission requirements rather than having to integrate every underlying electronic component themselves.

For military users, the implications extend across multiple mission areas. EW, radar, SATCOM, and counter-UAS systems operate across different frequency bands, but they share the need for efficient RF amplification, signal conditioning, and reliable performance under demanding environmental conditions.

The company’s acquired RF capabilities from the acquisitions mentioned above include technologies with a storied history in counter-improvised explosive device (IED) systems dating to the early 2000s – particularly the Counter Radio-Controlled Improvised Explosive Device Electronic Warfare (CREW) system that jammed RF signals that set off IEDs. That heritage also informs applications involving counter-UAS and other EW missions.

Another important requirement for today’s military electronics is delivering greater RF power from smaller packages while controlling thermal loads. Frontgrade provides efficient power amplifiers for small spaces that operate in high-thermal environments. Those attributes’ constraints are especially significant in space, where spacecraft cannot rely on the cooling approaches commonly available in terrestrial data centers and communications facilities.

The result is an engineering tradeoff in which power output, efficiency, packaging, and thermal performance is considered together rather than optimized independently.

**Building adaptability into the hardware**

The next step is making RF electronics easier to modify after the initial system design has been completed. Graves distinguishes between scalability, which generally involves expanding an existing capability, and extensibility, which allows proven technology to be adapted for different operating environments and mission requirements.

Common design elements developed for space, counter-UAS, and EW applications can serve as starting points for related systems. Using previously qualified modules can reduce development effort and enable suppliers to meet more demanding deployment schedules.

For example, that philosophy informs the design of Frontgrade’s power amplifiers. Rather than treating an amplifier as fixed hardware with a single operating configuration, Frontgrade is incorporating telemetry, health monitoring, and software-controlled features that allow performance to be adjusted to changing requirements. Those features support changes in power efficiency and waveform characteristics without necessarily requiring a hardware replacement.

Graves described these devices as “smart” power amplifiers, with controls intended to make the RF chain more responsive to operational requirements. The distinction becomes critical for equipment deployed in space as physical access to satellites is generally unavailable, making software adaptability considerably more important.

With having software-controlled RF capabilities, operators can adapt to interference and maintain communications links needed to deliver information to warfighters. The goal is to preserve the usefulness of existing hardware as threats and mission requirements evolve rather than treating every new requirement as a reason to redesign the system.

title: Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal

content:
别让中国的间谍活动成为美国自己的目标博客 | 2026 年 11 月 12 日 | ITIF跳到内容
不要让中国的间谍活动成为美国自己的目标
据称中国针对英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋的情报行动最终可能给美国带来的损失远远超过中国的损失。英伟达失去了长期担任的首席执行官，美国投资者损失了数千亿美元的市值，美国决策者正在考虑对芯片出口实施新的限制，这可能会进一步损害美国科技公司的利益。美国在阻止中国军方获取先进人工智能芯片方面拥有合法利益，但它不应该允许所谓的中国间谍活动推动其采取削弱本国半导体行业的政策。
这场争议始于有报道称，美国情报机构怀疑新加坡 Megaspeed International 前高管 Alice Huang 为中国国家安全部工作。据报道，调查人员怀疑她与黄仁勋建立了关系，以收集有关英伟达及其运营的信息。黄仁勋承认与她有婚外关系，并分别面临与向他汇报的英伟达员工发生另一段关系的报道。 11月12日，英伟达宣布黄仁勋在领导公司33年后辞去首席执行官一职，并任命首席财务官科莱特·克雷斯(Colette Kress)为临时首席执行官。
这些指控引发了严重的国家安全担忧。据报道，Megaspeed 购买了价值约 48 亿美元的 Nvidia 硬件。美国当局怀疑该公司正在帮助中国客户规避对先进人工智能芯片的限制。据报道，在 2024 年对马来西亚设施的检查中，商务部官员发现 Nvidia 硬件仍然装在盒子里，而不是安装在数据中心，引发了人们对这些设备可能运往中国的担忧。
这些指控仍在调查中。 Megaspeed 否认有不当行为，表示正在配合美国当局的检查，并委托一家美国律师事务所对其芯片库存和出口管制做法进行独立审查。新加坡当局也在调查该公司。
如果这些指控属实，中国将取得重大成就：扰乱美国最重要的科技公司之一，并有可能获得敏感的商业信息。即使没有证据表明英伟达的商业机密或国家安全信息遭到泄露，损失也已经是巨大的。英伟达失去了长期的领导者，其股东看到数千亿美元的市值蒸发，该公司在服务国际客户的能力方面面临着新的不确定性。直接的经济成本落在了一家美国公司及其投资者身上。
中国自己的半导体战略使这一情况尤其具有启发性。北京希望减少对美国技术的依赖，建立国内芯片产业。它越来越多地利用采购限制和政府指导来引导中国企业转向国内加工商。例如，据报道，2025 年 11 月，中国当局指示国家资助的数据中心使用国产人工智能芯片。 2026 年 1 月，中国当局也不鼓励购买 Nvidia 的 H200 处理器，尽管中国公司对此表现出强烈兴趣。

【原文 English Original】
Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal | Blogs | Nov 12, 2026 | ITIFSkip to content
Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal
An alleged Chinese intelligence operation targeting Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang could end up costing the United States far more than it costs China. Nvidia has lost its longtime chief executive, American investors have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and U.S. policymakers are considering new restrictions on chip exports that could further undermine American technology companies. The United States has a legitimate interest in preventing the Chinese military from acquiring advanced AI chips, but it should not allow an alleged Chinese espionage operation to push it toward policies that weaken its own semiconductor industry.
The controversy began with reports that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, of working for China's Ministry of State Security. Investigators reportedly suspected she had cultivated a relationship with Jensen Huang to gather information about Nvidia and its operations. Jensen Huang acknowledged having an extramarital relationship with her and separately faced reports of another relationship with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. On November 12, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO after 33 years leading the company and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
The allegations raise serious national security concerns. Megaspeed reportedly purchased approximately $4.8 billion in Nvidia hardware. U.S. authorities suspected that the company was helping Chinese customers circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips. During a 2024 inspection of a Malaysian facility, Commerce Department officials reportedly found Nvidia hardware still packed in boxes rather than installed in data centers, raising concerns that the equipment might be destined for China.
These allegations remain under investigation. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing, says it is cooperating with inspections by U.S. authorities, and has commissioned an independent review by a U.S. law firm of its chip inventory and export-control practices. Singaporean authorities are also investigating the company.
If the allegations are true, China will have achieved something significant: disrupting one of America's most important technology companies and potentially gaining access to sensitive commercial information. Even without evidence that Nvidia's trade secrets or national security information were compromised, the damage is already substantial. Nvidia has lost its longtime leader, its shareholders have seen hundreds of billions of dollars in market value evaporate, and the company faces renewed uncertainty about its ability to serve international customers. The immediate economic costs are falling on an American company and its investors.
China's own semiconductor strategy makes the situation particularly revealing. Beijing wants to reduce dependence on American technology and build a domestic chip industry. It has increasingly used procurement restrictions and government guidance to steer Chinese companies toward domestic processors. In November 2025, for example, Chinese authorities reportedly directed state-funded data centers to use domestically produced AI chips. In January 2026, Chinese authorities also discouraged purchases of Nvidia's H200 processors, despite strong interest from Chinese companies.
Yet Chinese companies continue to seek access to Nvidia's most powerful processors, including through overseas data centers. This reflects a distinction between Beijing's long-term industrial ambitions and the immediate commercial interests of Chinese technology companies. China wants its domestic chipmakers to capture the market, but its AI developers still benefit from access to the best available hardware.
Congress now risks helping China achieve its goals. One proposal, the Remote Access Security Act (RASA), would expand export controls to cover foreign access to restricted U.S. technology through cloud computing services. The legislation addresses a legitimate concern: Chinese companies could potentially rent computing capacity overseas even when they cannot legally purchase the underlying chips. But an overly broad law could also create uncertainty for legitimate international cloud services and impose new compliance costs on American technology companies.
The AI OVERWATCH Act and Chip Security Act would go further. The AI OVERWATCH Act would require licenses for certain advanced-chip exports to countries of concern and give Congress advance notice of proposed sales, with an opportunity to block them through a joint resolution. That process could make access to U.S. chips subject to greater political uncertainty, even for transactions that meet existing export-control requirements. The Chip Security Act would require security mechanisms to help verify whether exported chips have been diverted, potentially including location trackers, on-site audits, or legal attestations. Such measures could help detect illicit transfers, but they could also raise concerns among legitimate international customers about monitoring, data security, and government access to information about their computing infrastructure. Both bills risk making U.S. technology less attractive to customers who have other options.
The United States should strengthen enforcement against companies and individuals that knowingly divert restricted chips. It should also improve verification of end users and investigate suspicious transactions. But Congress should be careful about creating new restrictions that unnecessarily limit legitimate commercial activity.
American semiconductor leadership depends heavily on private-sector investment in research and development. Nvidia and other U.S. chipmakers spend billions developing successive generations of increasingly powerful processors. International sales generate revenue that supports this investment, helps companies achieve economies of scale, and finances future innovation. Overly restricting access to the Chinese market would weaken an important source of commercial demand while giving Chinese competitors more opportunities to improve their products and gain market share.
China has an obvious interest in reducing its dependence on American semiconductors. But its own record of economic espionage and trade-secret theft—including documented efforts to steal semiconductor technology—underscores why the allegations deserve serious attention. President Trump should put the issue on the agenda when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month.
Any proven violations should carry meaningful consequences. But a domestic response that hurts American companies, reduces their global markets, and encourages customers to adopt Chinese alternatives would compound the damage. China may have played Jensen Huang. Congress should make sure it does not play into Beijing's hands.

资助机会通知 (NOFO)：在斯威士兰举办 2027 GCTF 研讨会 资助机会通知 (NOFO) 在斯威士兰美国台湾学院举办 2027 G CTF 研讨会 机会编号：GCTF-TAIPEI-FY2 7 -00 1 申请截止日期：202 年 11 月 23 日 6 日晚上 11:59 （台北时间） A. 基本信息 1. 概述 资助方式：合作协议。合作协议包括局或大使馆实质性参与项目的计划实施。下文 C.2 节包含实质性参与的示例。项目实施期限：拟建项目应于202年5月31日前完成 7．本通知视资金情况而定。公共外交部门保留在被认为符合美国政府最佳利益的情况下授予少于或超过所述资金的权利，具体取决于资金的可用性和指定拨款官员的批准。 2. 执行摘要 美国在台协会 (AIT) 公共外交部门 (PDS) 宣布开展一项合作协议公开竞赛，以支持 2027 年第一季度或第二季度在斯威士兰规划和实施全球合作与培训框架 (GCTF) 区域特许经营研讨会。在资金允许的情况下，AIT 打算授予一份约 20 万美元的合作协议来实施该计划。
全球合作与培训框架（GCTF）是一个国际能力建设平台，汇集了政府官员、技术专家、行业代表、学者和民间社会代表，交流实践经验并加强应对区域和全球挑战的合作。GCTF由台湾和美国于2015年成立，此后扩大到包括日本、澳大利亚、加拿大和英国作为合作伙伴。拟议的研讨会“加强南部非洲的网络安全和数字治理”预计将于 2027 年第一季度或第二季度在斯威士兰举行。该计划将重点关注加强网络安全弹性、改善数字治理、保护关键数字基础设施、应对新出现的网络威胁以及促进安全和可信的数字转型。它将为参与者提供一个交流实践经验、确定共同挑战、加强专业网络和区域合作的平台。该研讨会预计将包括来自至少八个非洲国家的代表，特别强调南部非洲的区域参与。第一天预计将有约 60 至 80 名参与者参加，活动内容包括全体讨论、专家演讲和实践交流。
预计第二天将有约 40 名参与者参加，其中可能包括重点技术讨论、互动练习、工作组会议和/或相关现场参观。该计划预计将汇集来自参与非洲国家的政府官员、网络安全和数字治理从业者、技术专家、私营部门代表、学者、民间社会代表和其他相关利益攸关方。来自美国、台湾和其他 GCTF 合作伙伴（包括日本、澳大利亚、加拿大）的主题专家

【原文 English Original】
Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO): Implementation of 2027 GCTF Workshop in Eswatini Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) Implementation of 2027 G CTF Workshop in Eswatini American Institute in Taiwan Opportunity number: GCTF-TAIPEI-FY2 7 -00 1 Application deadline: November 23 , 202 6 , at 11:59 p.m. (Taipei Time)   A. Basic Information 1. Overview Funding Instrument Type: C ooperative agreement . Cooperative agreements include substantial involvement of the bureau or embassy in program implementation of the project. Examples of substantial involvement are included in section C.2 below. Project Performance Period : Proposed projects should be completed by May 31 , 202 7 . This notice is subject to availability of funding. The Public Diplomacy Section reserves the right to award less or more than the funds described under circumstances deemed to be in the best interest of the U.S. government, pending the availability of funds and approval of the designated grants officer. 2. Executive Summary The American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) Public Diplomacy Section (PDS) announces an open competition for a cooperative agreement to support the planning and implementation of a Global Cooperation and Training Framework (GCTF) regional franchise workshop in Eswatini in the first or second quarter of 2027. Subject to the availability of funding, AIT intends to award one cooperative agreement of approximately USD 200,000 to implement this program. The Global Cooperation and Training Framework (GCTF) is an international capacity-building platform that brings together government officials, technical experts, industry representatives, academics, and civil society representatives to exchange practical experiences and strengthen cooperation in addressing regional and global challenges. The GCTF was established by Taiwan and the United States in 2015 and has since expanded to include Japan, Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom as Partners. The proposed workshop, “Strengthening Cybersecurity and Digital Governance in Southern Africa,” is expected to take place in Eswatini during the first or second quarter of 2027. The program will focus on strengthening cybersecurity resilience, improving digital governance, protecting critical digital infrastructure, addressing emerging cyber threats, and promoting secure and trusted digital transformation. It will provide a platform for participants to exchange practical experiences, identify common challenges, and strengthen professional networks and regional cooperation. The workshop is expected to include representatives from at least eight African countries, with a particular emphasis on regional participation from Southern Africa. Approximately 60 to 80 participants are expected to participate in the first day of the program, which will feature plenary discussions, expert presentations, and practical exchanges. A smaller group of approximately 40 participants is expected to participate in the second day, which may include focused technical discussions, interactive exercises, working-group sessions, and/or relevant site visits. The program is expected to bring together government officials, cybersecurity and digital governance practitioners, technical experts, private-sector representatives, academics, civil society representatives, and other relevant stakeholders from participating African countries. Subject-matter experts from the United States, Taiwan, and other GCTF Partners, including Japan, Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom, may also be invited to contribute relevant international expertise and practical experience. The selected recipient will serve as AIT’s implementation partner and will be responsible for comprehensive program and logistical support, including venue and lodging coordination, participant management, travel arrangements for designated participants and speakers, ground transportation, interpretation and audiovisual services, workshop materials, vendor coordination, monitoring and evaluation, and required grant reporting. Travel expenses for U.S. Government officials invited by the U.S. Government and Taiwan-supported speakers will be funded separately and should not be included in the recipient’s proposed budget. AIT and GCTF partners will provide overall policy guidance, strategic direction, and substantive oversight throughout program planning and implementation. Eligible applicants include nonprofit organizations, educational institutions, professional associations, think tanks, private-sector organizations with relevant international program management experience, public international organizations where eligible under applicable U.S. Government regulations, and other eligible organizations with demonstrated capacity to organize international conferences or capacity-building programs and administer U.S. Government assistance awards. This cooperative agreement is intended to strengthen practical cybersecurity capacity and digital governance cooperation in Southern Africa, expand professional and institutional connections among participating countries, and advance the GCTF as a platform for practical international capacity building, technical exchange, and sustained regional cooperation. B. Eligibility 1. Eligible Applicants The following organizations are eligible to apply: Not-for-profit organizations , including non-governmental organizations (NGOs), think tanks, and civil society organizations Educational institutions , including universities and research institutions Professional associations and nonprofit organizations with demonstrated experience managing international conferences or capacity-building programs Private-sector organizations with demonstrated experience organizing international conferences or implementing international exchange programs Public international organizations , where eligible under applicable U.S. Government regulations Organizations may sub-contract with other entities, but only one entity, from the eligible categories of organizations listed above, can be the prime recipient of the award. When sub-contracting with other entities, the responsibilities of each entity must be clearly defined in the proposal. For more information on the difference between sub-contract and sub-recipient, please refer to 2 CFR 200 .331 . 2. Cost Sharing or Matching Cost sharing is not required . 3. Other Eligibility Requirements All organizations must have a Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) issued via SAM.gov as well as a valid registration in SAM.gov. Please see Section D.3 for more information. Individuals are not required to have a UEI or be registered in SAM.gov. Applicants are only allowed to submit one proposal per organization. If more than one proposal is submitted from an organization, all proposals from that institution will be considered ineligible for funding. 4. This opportunity will not support: Projects relating to partisan political activity; Charitable or development activities; including direct social services such as medical, psychological, and/or humanitarian support Construction projects; Projects that support specific religious activities; Fund-raising campaigns; Lobbying for specific legislation or programs Scientific research or surveys; Commercial projects; Projects intended primarily for the growth or institutional development of the organization; Projects that duplicate existing projects; Illegal activities C. Program Description 1. Project Background, Goals, and Objectives Project Background The Global Cooperation and Training Framework (GCTF) is an international capacity-building platform established by Taiwan and the United States in 2015. Japan joined as a full partner in 2019, followed by Australia in 2021, Canada in 2023, and the United Kingdom in 2025. Through workshops and other capacity-building activities, GCTF brings together government officials, technical experts, industry representatives, and civil society representatives to exchange practical experience, strengthen professional networks, and develop approaches to shared regional and global challenges. As governments and societies become increasingly dependent on digital technologies and interconnected systems, cybersecurity and effective digital governance have become important elements of economic development, public-service delivery, critical infrastructure resilience, and public trust. Recent research documents that scam syndicates displaced from Southeast Asian epicenters, including Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia, are actively pivoting to Africa, with documented raids in nine African countries and growing evidence of scam infrastructure, including online gambling platforms used as cover for fraud operations, gray business Telegram groups openly advertising scam facilities, and unregulated cryptocurrency services establishing footholds across the continent. Countries across Southern Africa face evolving cybersecurity and cybercrime challenges while also seeking to expand digital services, strengthen institutional capacity, and develop governance frameworks that support secure and trusted digital transformation. The proposed GCTF regional workshop in Eswatini will provide a platform for government officials, cybersecurity and the digital governance practitioners, technical experts, private-sector representatives, academics, civil society representatives, and other relevant stakeholders from across Africa to exchange practical experiences and strengthen professional and institutional connections. The workshop is expected to include representatives from at least eight African countries, with particular emphasis on participation from Southern Africa. The program will draw on expertise and practical experience from participating African countries as well as the United States, Taiwan, and other GCTF partners, as appropriate. Through expert presentations, policy and technical discussions, interactive exchanges, and other practical activities, the workshop will address shared challenges and identify approaches that participating countries may adapt to their respective national and institutional contexts. Strengthening cybersecurity capacity and secure digital governance in Southern Africa also advances U.S. security and economic interests. Cyber threats, cyber-enabled crime, and vulnerabilities in interconnected digital systems increasingly cross-national borders and can affect American citizens, businesses, and critical infrastructure. By strengthening the ability of partner countries to prevent, identify, respond to, and recover from cyber threats, this program can help reduce vulnerabilities that may be exploited by transnational criminal networks and other malicious cyber actors. The workshop will also strengthen U.S. engagement with African partners on secure and resilient digital ecosystems, promote cooperation and information sharing among governments and technical experts, and expand relationships between African stakeholders and the United States and other GCTF partners. Through practical capacity building and sustained professional networks, the program will support a more secure and resilient regional digital environment while advancing shared interests in cybersecurity, economic security, and trusted digital development. Project Goal: The goal of this project is to strengthen cybersecurity resilience and digital governance capacity in Southern Africa by facilitating practical knowledge exchange, regional cooperation, and sustained professional engagement among participating countries and international partners, while advancing shared U.S. and partner interests in a more secure, resilient, and trusted digital environment. Project Objectives: The project will pursue the following objectives: Strengthen Cybersecurity Capacity and Resilience: Enhance participants’ knowledge of practical approaches to preventing, preparing for, responding to, and recovering from cybersecurity threats and incidents, with a specific focus on basic cyber hygiene, national cyber resilience, digital trust, and the development of a secure digital ecosystem aligned with global standards and best practices. Advance Effective and Secure Digital Governance: Promote the exchange of policies, practices, institutional approaches, and lessons learned that support secure, trusted, resilient, and inclusive digital governance and digital transformation. Promote Regional Cooperation and Information Sharing: Strengthen professional and institutional connections among participating African countries and encourage greater cross-border cooperation, information sharing, and coordination in addressing shared cybersecurity and digital governance challenges. Facilitate Practical International Exchange: Connect African policymakers and practitioners with relevant expertise and practical experience from participating African countries, the United States, Taiwan, and other GCTF partner countries, including Japan, Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom, as appropriate to the workshop agenda. Support Sustainable Professional Networks and Follow-on Cooperation: Encourage participants to identify practical opportunities for continued professional engagement, knowledge sharing, and future cooperation beyond the workshop. 2. Substantial Involvement This award will require substantial involvement from the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT ) and the U . S . Embassy in Eswatini . AIT will approve all key aspects of the workshop, including but not limited to venue selection, flight and hotel arrangements, ground transportation, lodging, visual designs, agenda, site visit locations, speaker and participant lists, catering and menus, conference room layout, lighting, and audio-visual setup. A searchable list can be found in the Federal Register: https://www.federalregister.gov/ . 2. Reporting Reporting Requirements: Recipients will be required to submit financial reports and program reports. The FADR requires tracking of foreign assistance activity data from budgeting, planning, and allocation through obligation and disbursement. Successful applicants will be required to report and draw down federal funding based on the appropriate FADR Data Elements, indicated within their award documentation. In cases of more than one FADR Data Element, typically program or sector and/or regions or country, the successful applicant will be required to maintain separate accounting records. If the federal share of the award will include more than $500,000 over the period of performance, insert the following language: Applicants should be aware of the post award reporting requirements reflected in 2 CFR 200 Appendix XII—Award Term and Condition for Recipient Integrity and Performance Matters . 3.Branding and Marking The Department of State, its programs, and U.S. Government funding and assistance should be easily identifiable to the Department’s global audiences. Recipients of federal assistance awards must follow the branding guidance published at Guidance for Contracts and Grants – U.S. Department of State Brand System. Branding policy exceptions are outlined in the U.S. Department of State Foreign Affairs Manual 10 FAM 416, Policy Exceptions. For more information, visit: https://brand.america.gov/ I. Other Information Guidelines for Budget Justification Personnel and Fringe Benefits: Describe the wages, salaries, and benefits of temporary or permanent staff who will be working directly for the applicant on the program, and the percentage of their time that will be spent on the program. Travel: Estimate the costs of travel and per diem for this program, for program staff, consultants or speakers, and participants/beneficiaries. Other Direct Costs: Describe other costs directly associated with the program, which do not fit in the other categories. For example, shipping costs for materials and equipment or applicable taxes. Organizations that have never had a NICRA may request indirect costs of 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) as defined in 2 CFR 200.1. “Cost Sharing” refers to contributions from the organization or other entities other than AIT. It also includes in-kind contributions such as volunteers’ time and donated venues. title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex- Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
zh_title: 大多数事情除了对相关人员而言并不重要。英伟达前首席执行官詹森的错误将震惊世界
